Who Will NOT Be Gukesh and Sindarov’s Seconds? Top Stories & Features Gukesh vs Sindarov: everything you need to know about the 2026 World Championship
 Sagar Shah November 16, 2026 · 5 min read In eight days, D. Gukesh sits down in Geneva to defend his World Championship title against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan. Both players will be 20 years old when Game 1 begins on 24 November, which makes this, in FIDE's words, "the youngest World Championship contest in history". In this article you get to know everything about the World Championship Match 2026.

 The match was first announced for 25 November to 15 December. In August, FIDE moved it forward to 22 November to 12 December | Graphic: FIDE The match at a glance
 Players
 D. Gukesh (India), World Champion, vs Javokhir Sindarov (Uzbekistan), challenger
 Venue
 Fondation Martin Bodmer, Cologny, Geneva, Switzerland
 Dates
 Opening ceremony 22 November; Game 1 on 24 November; Game 14 on 11 December; tiebreaks, if needed, 12 December
 Games
 Up to 14 classical games; first to 7.5 points wins
 Start time
 3 pm in Geneva, which is 7:30 pm IST 
 Prize fund
 US $2.5 million
 Title sponsor
 Salesforce
 Geneva hosts the first World Championship match in Switzerland since Brissago in 2004. FIDE Interim President Viswanathan Anand called the Fondation Martin Bodmer "a fitting venue for this match." Get to know more about the venue here . The main sponsor of the event is Salesforce and the General Partner is Freedom.
 India, the USA and Cyprus also showed interest in hosting, but the match went to the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva | Photo: FIDE How did we get here?
 Singapore, December 2024: D. Gukesh with the title he now defends in Geneva | Photo: FIDE World Championship 2024 Gukesh became the 18th World Champion at the age of 18, beating Ding Liren in their 2024 match. Sindarov earned his shot the hard way. He won the 2025 FIDE World Cup to qualify for the Candidates, and then won the Candidates in Cyprus (28 March to 16 April 2026) with 10/14, six wins and no losses, a clear 1.5 points ahead of Anish Giri. Fabiano Caruana was third. R. Praggnanandhaa, India's representative, finished on 6/14.
 Round 13 in Cyprus: Sindarov's draw with Anish Giri sealed the Candidates with a round to spare | Photo: FIDE Candidates 2026 Sindarov became a grandmaster at 12. Tomorrow we tell his full story for Indian readers: who he is, where he comes from, and why he is so dangerous.

 Tiebreaks (if needed) and closing ceremony
 The rhythm is three games, then a rest day. The match ends as soon as one player reaches 7.5 points, so the later games may never be played.
 A small detail: Sindarov turns 21 on 8 December, the day of Game 12.
 Rules that you should know
 Time control. Each player gets 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, then 30 more minutes for the rest of the game, with 30 seconds added per move from move 41.
 Colours. Colours are drawn for Game 1. The player with White in Game 1 has White in all odd-numbered games, and Black in the even ones.
 No quick draws. The players cannot agree a draw before Black's 40th move. Before that, a draw is possible only by threefold repetition or stalemate, claimed through the Chief Arbiter or Deputy.
 Tiebreaks. If it is 7-7 after 14 games, the match goes to 12 December:
 Four rapid games at 15 minutes plus 10 seconds per move.
 If still level, two games at 10 minutes plus 5 seconds.
 If still level, two blitz games at 3 minutes plus 2 seconds.
 If still level, single 3+2 games, colours reversed each time, until someone wins one.
 Reserves. If either player cannot play, Anish Giri, the Candidates runner-up, takes his place, with Fabiano Caruana next in line.
 The money
 The prize fund is US $2.5 million, net of local taxes. Each player gets US $200,000 for every game he wins, and the rest is split equally.
 There is one exception. If the match is decided in the tiebreaks, or ends by the narrowest classical margin (7.5-6.5 with 13 decisive games, or 8-6 with all 14 games decisive), the winner gets US $1.3 million and the loser US $1.2 million.
 The teaching moment here is simple: every win is worth US $200,000 on its own. In a match where both players are fighting for a crown, the prize structure also rewards taking risks.
 Who is the favourite?
 On paper, Sindarov. On the November FIDE list he is world number 4 at 2782, while Gukesh is 2710 and number 26, a gap of 72 points. His average performance across his first four major classical events of 2026 was 2837. In their three classical games so far, Sindarov leads 2-0 with one draw: he won at the 2018 Moscow Open and the 2022 Sharjah Masters, and their game at Tata Steel in January 2026 was drawn. We will show you those games, with their best moments on the board, in the coming days.
 But a World Championship match is not a rating list. Garry Kasparov, speaking in Antwerp on 21 October , gave Gukesh slightly better chances on experience: "You can hardly beat Gukesh." Gukesh has done this before, and Sindarov has not.
 The seconds
 Sindarov works with his longtime coach, IM Roman Vidonyak . Gukesh has his coach Grzegorz Gajewski in his camp. There will be a long list of strong players who will be helping both Gukesh and Sindarov but this has not been made clear as yet. And for a lighter take, here is who will NOT be their seconds .
 Where to follow it
 ChessBase India will be in Geneva from the opening ceremony, with daily reports after every game. We will also have a live broadcast at the Habitat, Mumbai where people can follow it LIVE just like they did in 2024. This will be streamed on our YouTube channel and will be in partnership with chess.com India and we will have 6 very cool commentators - Tania Sachdev, Amruta Mokal, Harshit Raja, Sahil Tickoo, Sahaj Grover and Sagar Shah.
